    Plugin guide

    Plugins add species, property equations, and reaction models to MultiSolid. Start with the smallest change you need: changing coefficients usually needs no Python; writing a new equation does.

    What you want to do Start here
    Change an existing species or reaction parameter Create a variant in the application
    Define a new species using the existing property equations Create a species plugin
    Write a new property equation or reaction rate Plugin authoring walkthrough
    Understand the files and Python API Authoring reference
    Use a plugin someone sent you Install and use a plugin
    Send your plugin to someone else Share and update plugins
    Fix a problem Troubleshooting

    The example walkthrough builds a complete plugin one file at a time. It starts with a species in YAML, then adds a Python property equation and a reaction. The examples use illustrative coefficients and kinetics; they are teaching material, not validated scientific models.

    Choose what to define

    A plugin is a folder containing manifest.yaml and, when needed, Python files. The manifest gives the plugin a name and describes what it provides. An exported .msplugin file packages that folder for sharing.

    Part Meaning Example
    Species A chemical identity, phase, molecular weight, and property definitions NH3 gas
    Correlation An equation that calculates a property from temperature Molar enthalpy and heat capacity
    Reaction family One or more reactions, with their stoichiometry and rate equations Ammonia synthesis
    Parameter A value that users can change without editing an equation A rate coefficient k

    You do not need to write Python for every species. Polynomial or Shomate heat capacity and quadratic gas viscosity are already available. Use the application forms or a manifest to supply their coefficients. Use Python when those equations cannot express your property model, or when you need a new rate law.

    Create a variant in the application

    This is the quickest way to try different coefficients for an existing model. You need only the desktop application and an open project.

    For example, to give nitrogen a different heat capacity:

    1. Open Plugins, beside Project in the menu bar.
    2. Expand the built-in definitions and select Nitrogen. Use the filter to find it if necessary.
    3. Choose Create variant… and enter a recognizable New plugin name, such as My nitrogen properties.
    4. Choose Polynomial Cp under Heat capacity / enthalpy. Set Tref (K) to 298.15, H at Tref (J/mol) to 0, and Cp coefficients a0, a1, … to 30, 0.004, 0.000001. These are illustrative values. Keep the chemical key N2 and phase gas to make this a nitrogen replacement.
    5. Save. The application checks the definition and creates an enabled plugin.
    6. Select the new plugin's Nitrogen definition and choose Use this as replacement…. Choose the existing nitrogen definition and review the affected cases before applying the change.

    The last step connects your definition to cases that already use nitrogen. If the project has no such cases, add the new definition in a case's Chemistry tab instead. Creating or enabling a plugin alone does not change any case.

    The same workflow works for reaction parameters: select a built-in reaction or family, choose Create variant…, edit its exposed values, and save. Select the family entry when replacing an existing family in cases. A reaction's editor exposes only its declared parameters; changing stoichiometry or adding a new rate equation requires Python authoring.

    Double-click a definition in your own plugin to edit it. Double-click a built-in definition to create a variant. Selecting a family shows all its parameters; selecting a reaction shows its parameter group when one is available. Shared parameters are marked. Reset shown values restores implementation defaults.

    Save checks and commits the edit. Invalid values remain in the editor with an explanation. Cancel, Escape, or closing the editor discards unsaved edits. Saving unchanged values does not create another copy.

    Create a species plugin

    For a new species, choose Plugins → Create plugin…, name it, then select the plugin and choose Add species…. The application generates the internal IDs. Fill in these fields:

    Field What to enter
    Name A readable label, such as Ammonia
    Chemical key The chemical identity used to match reaction roles, such as NH3
    Phase gas or solid
    Molecular weight kg/mol, so 17.03 g/mol becomes 0.01703 kg/mol
    Minimum / maximum T The temperature interval in K for which your definition is intended
    Heat capacity / enthalpy An equation type, its coefficients, and reference enthalpy
    Gas viscosity Quadratic coefficients in the displayed SI units; required for gas species
    Scientific source / Notes Data source, fit assumptions, and limitations

    Save, then add another species if needed. A plugin may contain several species. Custom enthalpy correlations already declared in that plugin also appear in the species form. Their parameters are editable there. Custom viscosity code and its configuration are edited in the source package.

    Prefer text files? Lesson 1 provides a complete manifest.yaml to copy. There is no Python file, build step, or metadata-generation step for that example.

    Property units and coefficient conventions

    Temperatures are in K, molecular weights in kg/mol, molar enthalpies in J/mol, heat capacities in J/(mol·K), and viscosities in Pa·s.

    The declared temperature_range documents the intended range. It does not clamp temperatures or stop a simulation outside that range. Check your case's results against the validity ranges of its selected definitions.

    Built-in equation Manifest model Parameters
    Polynomial heat capacity builtin:polynomial coefficients, t_ref, h_form_ref
    Shomate heat capacity builtin:shomate a0 through a4, t_ref, h_form_ref
    Quadratic gas viscosity builtin:quadratic_viscosity a0, a1, a2, t_ref

    For polynomial Cp, with ΔT = T − t_ref:

    Cp(T) = a0 + a1 ΔT + a2 ΔT² + …
h(T)  = h_form_ref + a0 ΔT + (a1/2) ΔT² + (a2/3) ΔT³ + …

    Coefficients are in ascending order. Coefficient ai has units J/(mol·K^(i+1)); three coefficients give quadratic Cp. These are powers of T − t_ref, so coefficients fitted to powers of T need conversion first.

    For Shomate Cp, τ = T / (1000 K) and Cp = a0 + a1 τ + a2 τ² + a3 τ³ + a4/τ². Coefficients use J/(mol·K). MultiSolid integrates this expression and anchors enthalpy at h_form_ref at t_ref; do not paste a different source's full enthalpy coefficient set into these fields.

    For quadratic viscosity, μ = a0 + a1 ΔT + a2 ΔT². The coefficients have units Pa·s, Pa·s/K, and Pa·s/K² respectively. Its reference temperature may differ from the enthalpy reference temperature.

    Use consistent enthalpy references across reacting species. See the model equations for how properties and reaction source terms enter the balances.

    Install and use a plugin

    1. Open the destination project and choose Plugins → Register plugin….
    2. Select the supplied .msplugin archive, or select manifest.yaml inside the plugin folder. Keep its Python files and resources beside it.
    3. A plugin using only built-in equations is checked and enabled immediately. For a Python plugin, select it and choose Enable, then allow its code if you trust its source. Wait for Checks passed.
    4. In your case's Chemistry tab, add the plugin's species or reaction family from the appropriate picker. Select the reactions you intend to run.
    5. Check the family Bindings… and supply the corresponding gas compositions in Program and solid loadings in Bed. + Species can add missing components; it does not supply their compositions or loadings.

    Registration copies the folder into the project. Later edits to the original folder do not update the project copy; register it again after editing. Normal desktop use does not require a separate Python installation or a pip command for the plugin.

    Replace a definition or add a separate component

    Use Use this as replacement… when you want an existing case component to use new properties. Select the new species or family in Plugins, then choose the existing definition it should replace. Review the listed ordinary cases and reusable definitions. Component IDs, family instance IDs, compositions, and role bindings are preserved.

    A replacement species must have the same chemical key and phase. A replacement family must have the same ordered gas/solid roles and reaction IDs. The action does not change study selections or saved runs.

    Adding both original water and a water variant in Chemistry creates two distinct components, each with its own ID, composition, and balance equation. Use Bindings… to choose which component serves each reaction role. Likewise, selecting two reaction variants makes their selected rates add; remove a family you do not want to run. The editor shows an applicability caution for overlapping reactions.

    Python approval and checks

    The browser reads the manifest without importing plugin Python. Check and Enable execute it in a separate process; the application asks for local code approval first. An enabled plugin copied from another computer may show Needs local approval: choose Allow code… and wait for the check to finish.

    Approved code runs with your user permissions. The worker is not a security sandbox, and passing checks does not establish safety or scientific accuracy. Approval covers code and included resources. Changing manifest parameter values does not request approval again; changing code or resources does.

    Check failures and details appear in the browser or editor. Cancel check stops a pending check. Checks validate package structure, parameter declarations, factory return types, reaction metadata, and basic property construction. They do not compare every numerical and symbolic expression or validate a reactor model.

    Share and update plugins

    To share the version you edited in the application, select its plugin entry and choose Export…. Send the resulting .msplugin file. The recipient registers it in their project. You can also share the entire project folder; its plugins travel with it, while Python approval stays on each computer.

    For updates, keep the same plugin id and register the new manifest or archive. The application asks before replacing changed contents. To keep two alternatives, use Create variant…, or give your source copy a new id before registering it. Changing just the display name does not create an independent plugin.

    Each project stores one current copy at plugins/<plugin-id>/current/. There is no revision selector and no required version increment. Edit your authoring folder and re-register, or use the application forms and export their result. Avoid treating the project copy as a live link to your source folder.

    Cases and studies use the current contents of their selected plugins. Changing a selected plugin makes previous results stale; a plugin edit alone does not require a new study baseline or a study rebuild. An unrelated plugin edit does not affect those results. Removing or disabling a plugin still used by inputs is blocked, with its users listed.

    Prepared runs keep copies of their selected plugins beside their input snapshot. Later edits cannot change that snapshot. Generated CLI batch cases also carry their selected plugin files. Include a source citation, applicable temperature range, assumptions, and any redistribution terms with a plugin you distribute.

    Authoring reference

    Follow the worked tutorial for complete files and commands. This section explains the contract when you adapt them to your own model. Python authoring commands use the source environment (online), with the repository root as the working directory.

    Files and names

    my_plugin/
├── manifest.yaml       # Identity, species, and implementation references
├── enthalpy.py         # Optional custom property equation
├── kinetics.py         # Optional reaction family and rates
├── data/               # Optional local resources
└── README.md           # Scientific basis and usage notes

    manifest.yaml must be at the root of the folder or archive. Reference a Python factory as module:function: kinetics:create calls create(parameters) in kinetics.py. A nested module can use models.kinetics:create.

    Manifest field Meaning
    id Stable plugin identity, such as my_ammonia
    name Human-readable plugin name
    description, source Purpose and provenance
    species Map from local species IDs to property definitions
    correlations Map from local correlation IDs to custom implementations
    mechanisms Map from local family IDs to kinetics implementations
    derived_from Optional attribution to an original definition

    format_version and api_version currently default to 1; version defaults to the string "1". The current workflow does not use version fields to select historical plugin contents.

    Plugin and local definition IDs start with a letter and use letters, digits, underscores, dots, or hyphens. Choose portable names, avoiding Windows device names and trailing dots. builtin is reserved as a plugin ID.

    Keep these three names distinct:

    Name Example Purpose
    Definition reference my_ammonia:NH3 Plugin ID plus local species ID
    Chemical key / reaction role NH3 Matches a species to a chemical role
    Case component ID NH3 or NH3_variant Identifies the component in case compositions and balances

    Two definitions can have the same chemical key but different references. Case bindings choose which selected component supplies that role. Quote YAML strings such as 'NO', including map keys, because the YAML reader interprets unquoted NO as a boolean.

    Write declarations once, generate browsing metadata

    The manifest lets the application show a Python plugin's parameters and reactions without importing its code. Authors write those declarations in Python, then generate their manifest copies. You do not need to maintain both by hand.

    1. Write PARAMETERS and create(parameters) in your Python module.
    2. Put its implementation reference in the manifest. For a correlation, also set kind to enthalpy or viscosity.
    3. Run generate_metadata(folder). It fills parameter declarations and, for a reaction family, the gas roles, solid roles, and reactions.
    4. Check the package, then register its completed manifest or exported archive.

    The tutorial build script performs metadata generation, checking, and packaging with one command. Generation imports your Python modules, executes reaction factories, and rewrites manifest.yaml; use it on your own authoring files. It is not needed for a species plugin that uses only built-in property equations. Changing Python parameter declarations or reaction metadata requires regeneration; changing a species' parameter values does not.

    Parameters and factories

    Import the supported types from packed_bed.plugins. Its exports include ParameterSpec, parameter_group, BaseCorrelation, PolynomialHeatCapacity, ShomateHeatCapacity, QuadraticViscosity, ReactionDefinition, ReactionFamily, and KineticsContext.

    Declare editable scalar parameters in a module-level dictionary:

    from packed_bed.plugins import ParameterSpec

PARAMETERS = {
    "k": ParameterSpec(
        0.001, "m^3 bed/(mol*s)",
        "Rate coefficient using concentrations per bed volume", minimum=0,
    ),
}

    Every parameter needs a default and unit or explicit dimensionless basis. Bounds are optional and inclusive. The factory receives validated, immutable values. Use factory arguments and context.parameters, rather than modifying global constants. Only declared parameters appear in the application editor.

    The three places parameters appear have different jobs:

    Location What it stores
    Python PARAMETERS and generated manifest declarations Defaults, units, descriptions, and bounds
    species.<id>.enthalpy.parameters or .viscosity.parameters Values for that species' correlation
    mechanisms.<id>.values Overrides for that plugin reaction family's declared defaults

    Two species can share correlation code and have different parameter values. The CO2/H2O example (online) demonstrates this. Dotted declarations created with parameter_group resolve into nested parameter mappings; for example, oxidation.k becomes parameters["oxidation"]["k"].

    Property equations

    A property factory returns a BaseCorrelation subclass. Implement these methods:

    Method Enthalpy correlation returns Viscosity correlation returns
    value(T) Numerical h in J/mol Numerical μ in Pa·s
    dae_expression(T) Symbolic h with units Symbolic μ with units
    cp_value(T) Numerical Cp in J/(mol·K) Not used
    cp_dae_expression(T) Symbolic Cp with units Not used

    Numerical methods accept scalar temperatures and NumPy arrays, preserving array shape. Symbolic methods accept DAETools expressions; use DAETools functions and unit-bearing constants there. Keep solver imports inside symbolic methods so metadata generation and ordinary numerical checks can run without the solver.

    Require dh/dT = Cp and h(t_ref) = h_ref. Check finite values over your intended range, positive Cp and viscosity where applicable, and agreement between the numerical and symbolic implementations. Registration is not a full scientific self-test. Lesson 2 includes a numerical consistency check.

    Reaction equations

    A kinetics factory returns a ReactionFamily with a name, reaction definitions, required gas and solid roles, and a map from each reaction ID to its rate function. The map needs exactly one callable for every reaction.

    A ReactionDefinition provides id, name, phase (gas_gas, gas_solid, or solid_solid), stoichiometry, required_species, and source_reference. Negative stoichiometric coefficients consume a species; positive ones produce it. Declare all species read by a rate in required_species, including catalysts or other non-stoichiometric dependencies. List catalysts in catalyst_species without including them in stoichiometry.

    The rate receives a KineticsContext. Use:

    • context.model and context.idx_cell for the local model state;
    • context.gas_index(role) and context.solid_index(role) for bound indices;
    • context.molecular_weight(role) for the selected component's molecular weight;
    • context.parameters for the immutable parameter values.

    Return a symbolic reaction-extent rate in mol/(m³ bed·s). The engine multiplies it by stoichiometric coefficients to form species sources. Do not return a species-consumption rate without accounting for that coefficient. State variables model.c_gas and model.c_sol are per total bed volume. If your rate law uses concentration per gas volume, convert using model.gasfrac. Rate orders come from your equation, independently of stoichiometry.

    reversible is descriptive metadata; the rate function must implement any reverse or equilibrium term. Document guards for negative trial concentrations and zero inventories. Use the case's resolved properties rather than a global property registry. See Lesson 3 for a complete factory and rate function, and the equations guide for the balance and energy conventions.

    Dependencies and resources

    Keep a plugin self-contained. Include any custom species and correlations its mechanisms need. The three supplied examples work independently; one plugin cannot rely on another plugin's implementation files.

    Use relative imports between included modules, such as from .helpers import rate_factor. Locate local data relative to __file__. Supported libraries are Python's standard library, numpy, scipy, yaml, pydantic, xarray, matplotlib, daetools, pyUnits, and the public packed_bed.plugins API. Users should not need plugin-specific pip installs or runtime downloads.

    Packages cannot include symlinks or additional native libraries/runtimes (.so, .dll, .pyd, .exe, .whl). Paths must be portable across supported platforms. The package limit is 100 MiB and 5,000 files. Write archives outside the source plugin folder so they do not become part of the package.

    Case YAML and engine integration

    The application writes these mappings for you. For hand-authored inputs, this chemistry.yaml fragment selects the supplied ammonia example:

    gas_species: [N2, H2, NH3]
species_definitions:
  NH3: example_ammonia:NH3
reaction_families: [ammonia]
mechanisms:
  ammonia:
    definition: example_ammonia:synthesis
reaction_ids: [ammonia/synthesis]

    Use my_ammonia:NH3 and my_ammonia:synthesis for the tutorial's own plugin. These are chemistry selections, not a complete reactor case. Supply the other case files and make the plugin available through the project or a descriptor.

    Program composition maps use case component IDs. When the role and component names differ, add a bindings map inside that mechanism selection, for example bindings: {N2: N2_variant, H2: H2, NH3: NH3} with N2_variant selected in gas_species. Solid components are selected in solids.yaml; their definition references also belong in chemistry.yaml's species_definitions map.

    Reaction IDs normally take the form <instance>/<local-reaction-id>. Existing built-in family instance names retain their legacy reaction IDs, including after a compatible replacement.

    load_case discovers a containing project and its current plugins. Saved run snapshots use their frozen copies. Standalone inputs can place definitions.json beside run.yaml:

    {
  "root": "relative/path/to/project",
  "lock": {
    "builtin": "<built-in SHA-256 fingerprint>",
    "plugins": {"my_ammonia": "<plugin SHA-256 content hash>"}
  }
}

    Here root is relative to the descriptor; the selected package is under plugins/my_ammonia/current/ within that root. The strings in angle brackets are placeholders, not valid hashes. Desktop snapshots and CLI batch generation write these descriptors for you. Batch cases use root: "." and carry their plugins.

    An exact lock checks both built-in definitions and selected plugin contents. Mismatches are rejected: use the matching application and plugin copies, or explicitly regenerate inputs against the current definitions. Inputs without an exact lock use current definitions. A descriptor does not grant local Python approval.

    For Python integration, select_definitions(chemistry, solids, catalogue) and materialize_definitions(selection, catalogue) in packed_bed.definitions (online) separate metadata selection from implementation loading. Materialization returns a DefinitionEnvironment with properties, reaction_network, rate_hooks, and selection. Pass it through load_case(..., definitions=environment) or resolve_case(..., definitions=environment). Case.definitions is authoritative; a supplied environment does not fill missing definitions from global built-ins. inspect_case and inspect_case_file return metadata-only CaseInputs for editors.

    Troubleshooting

    What you see What to do
    Plugin is enabled, but the case still uses the old properties Select the new definition in Chemistry or use Use this as replacement….
    No compatible replacement appears Select a species or family entry. Check that an ordinary case or reusable definition uses the old definition and that chemical key/phase or family roles/reaction IDs match.
    Editing the source files has no effect Register the updated manifest.yaml again; the project holds a copy.
    A new copy replaces my previous plugin Give it a different top-level id; changing only name keeps its identity.
    A parameter is missing from the editor Declare it in Python PARAMETERS, regenerate metadata, then re-register. For existing declared values, edit species parameters or mechanism values.
    Python declarations or reaction metadata differ from the manifest Run the tutorial build script after editing declarations, then register the generated package.
    NO is rejected as a species key Quote 'NO' wherever it occurs in YAML.
    Needs local approval Select the plugin and choose Allow code… on this computer.
    Missing implementation or unsupported import Include the referenced .py file, use relative imports for your own modules, and use supported libraries.
    Property check rejects returned values Ensure numerical methods accept arrays and return finite arrays of the same shape. Basic checks sample 300 K and 1000 K; also test your declared range yourself.
    Missing species or ambiguous roles Add the needed components, then set Bindings… and their compositions/loadings.
    Remove or Disable is blocked Replace or remove its uses in the cases, reusable definitions, and study baselines listed by the application.
    Saved input fingerprint or hash mismatch Use the recorded application/plugin contents or explicitly regenerate inputs; do not alter the lock to conceal the mismatch.

    For a larger scientific package with provenance and fitted kinetics, see the waste iron plugin. The manifest contract is in schema.py (online), checking and metadata generation in check.py (online), and packaging in storage.py (online).
